# Matthew 15 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## vv. 1-2 — Pharisees and Scribes Challenge Jesus on Hand-Washing

**Traditional Reading:** An official delegation of scribes and Pharisees came from Jerusalem to investigate Jesus. They accused His disciples not of breaking Scripture, but of breaking the "tradition of the elders" — the oral law (Mishnah) handed down by past rabbis. The issue was ceremonial washing before meals, not hygiene. The Pharisees believed contact with Gentiles or unclean persons in the marketplace could convey ritual defilement, requiring elaborate washings (water poured over hands in a specific manner). According to rabbinic teaching, eating with unwashed hands was as serious as sexual immorality and could merit excommunication. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org; Gill on StudyLight.org; PreceptAustin.org)

- "These were from Jerusalem — an official delegation from headquarters, sent to confound the new Teacher" (Spurgeon, cited at PreceptAustin.org).
- "What the Pharisees insisted on was not cleanliness as such, but the avoidance of ceremonial pollution. They shrank not from dirt, but from defilement" (Ellicott on StudyLight.org).
- The Jewish Mishnah contained no fewer than 30 chapters on the cleansing of vessels (PreceptAustin.org, citing various sources).

## v. 3 — Jesus' Counter-Question

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus did not defend His disciples directly. Instead, He went on the offensive with an *argumentum ad hominem*: "Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?" His point: if the disciples broke a human rule, the Pharisees broke a divine command — a far graver offence. The very tradition they used to keep the law actually caused them to break it. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org; Gill on StudyLight.org)

- Jesus' reply was a "just recrimination," showing that the disciples were at most guilty of a human precept while the leaders were guilty of breaking a divine command (Gill on StudyLight.org).

## vv. 4-6 — The Corban Example

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus cited the fifth commandment ("Honour your father and mother," Exodus 20:12) and the death-penalty for cursing parents (Exodus 21:17). The Pharisees' tradition allowed a man to declare his resources "Corban" (a gift devoted to God), thereby legally shielding them from parental claims. The man did not actually have to give the property to the temple; the vow simply blocked his parents from benefiting. Thus the command to honour parents was "nullified" by tradition. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org; Gill on StudyLight.org)

- Ellicott explains the loophole in detail: the time of fulfilling the consecration vow was left to the man's own discretion, and no one could call him to account for delay. "With this loophole, the Corban practice became an easy method of evading natural obligations." (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)
- Gill cites extensive rabbinic sources showing the form of the vow: "Corban, whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me" — meaning, "Let anything I have that might benefit you be as Corban (dedicated and forbidden to you)." (Gill on StudyLight.org)
- Honour includes material support: "Our Saviour here also let us know, that the fifth commandment obligeth children to relieve their parents in their necessity" (Poole, cited at EnduringWord.com).

**Denominational Note — Reformed / Matthew Henry:** "Additions to God's laws reflect upon his wisdom, as if he had left out something which was needed, and which man could supply; in one way or other they always lead men to disobey God." (Matthew Henry on BibleHub.com)

## vv. 7-9 — Hypocrites! Isaiah's Prophecy Applied

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus called them "hypocrites" and quoted Isaiah 29:13. Their worship was lip-service; their hearts were far from God. They taught "as doctrines the commandments of men" — elevating human traditions to the level of divine revelation. Worship based on human authority is worthless ("in vain"). (EnduringWord.com; Matthew Henry on BibleHub.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

- Ellicott notes that "doctrines" here means "precepts taught as binding," not merely articles of belief. The "commandments" are single, special rules contrasted with God's broad commandment. (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)
- Gill points out that one rabbinic source said, "If the hypocrites of the world were divided into ten parts, nine of them would belong to Jerusalem" (Gill on StudyLight.org).

**Denominational Note — Baptist (Spurgeon):** "Religion based on human authority is worthless; we must worship the true God in the way of his own appointing, or we do not worship him at all." (Spurgeon, cited at PreceptAustin.org)

## vv. 10-11 — What Really Defiles

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus turned from the leaders to the crowd and stated a revolutionary principle: defilement is not about what enters the mouth (ceremonially unclean food or hands) but what comes out of it. This undercut the entire Levitical purity system. As France notes, these words "made the ultimate abandonment of the Old Testament food-laws by the church inevitable." (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

- Ellicott comments: "He removed the case... to another court... and turned from the disputes and traditions of the schools to the unperverted conscience of the common people." (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)
- Even after Pentecost, Peter still boasted he had "never eaten anything common or unclean" (Acts 10:14) — so slow were the disciples to grasp this. (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

## vv. 12-14 — The Pharisees Offended; Blind Guides

**Traditional Reading:** The disciples were concerned that the Pharisees were offended. Jesus was unperturbed. He said every plant not planted by the Father will be uprooted — connecting to the parable of the wheat and tares (Matthew 13). Pharisaism was not of God and would perish. "Let them alone" — no need to fight them; their system would collapse under its own weight. They were "blind leaders of the blind," a phrase that in Romans 2:19 was actually the rabbis' own ideal description of themselves. Now Jesus turned it against them: their blindness was self-chosen (cf. Matthew 13:15). (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

- Ellicott sees in the "ditch" a prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem: "We have but to read the Jewish historian's account of the years that preceded the destruction of Jerusalem to see what the 'ditch' was towards which teachers and people were alike blindly hastening." (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)
- "I pity the poor people, for whilst the blind lead the blind they both fall into a ditch. An ignorant and unfaithful ministry is the greatest plague God can send amongst a people." (Poole, cited at EnduringWord.com)
- "There was no need for the disciples to combat the Pharisees, they would be uprooted in the natural order of things by the inevitable consequences of their own course." (Spurgeon, cited at EnduringWord.com)

## vv. 15-20 — The Heart as the Source of Defilement

**Traditional Reading:** Peter asked for an explanation (calling it a "parable"). Jesus expressed gentle exasperation: "Are you also still without understanding?" He explained plainly: food enters the stomach and is eliminated — a purely physical process that cannot cause moral defilement. But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and *that* defiles. The list of heart-evils — evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, slander — reveals our fallen nature. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

- "Murders begin not with the dagger, but with the malice of the soul. Adulteries and fornications are first gloated over in the heart before they are enacted by the body." (Spurgeon, cited at EnduringWord.com)
- Ellicott notes the list ascends from inward "thoughts" to "blasphemies" which "directly or indirectly, have God and not man for their object" — possibly alluding to the Pharisees' blasphemy against the Son of Man in Matthew 12:24. (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)
- The phrase "is eliminated" uses a deliberately blunt, vulgar term: "A vulgar word and a vulgar subject which Jesus would gladly have avoided, but He forces Himself to speak of it for the sake of His disciples." (Bruce, cited at EnduringWord.com)

**Denominational Note — Reformed (Matthew Henry):** "It is the heart that is desperately wicked (Jer 17:9), for there is no sin in word or deed, which was not first in the heart... When Christ teaches, he will show men the deceitfulness and wickedness of their own hearts." (Matthew Henry on BibleHub.com)

## vv. 21-22 — Jesus Withdraws to Tyre and Sidon; the Canaanite Woman

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus left Jewish territory and went about 50 miles (80 km) to the Gentile region of Tyre and Sidon — the only recorded instance of Him travelling beyond Israel's borders (except possibly through Sidon on the return, per Mark 7:31). A Canaanite woman (Mark calls her Syro-Phoenician) approached Him, crying "Lord, Son of David, have mercy on me!" Her use of the Messianic title "Son of David" is striking: she, a Gentile and descendant of Israel's ancient enemies, recognised Jesus as the Jewish Messiah. She interceded for her demon-possessed daughter, making her daughter's need her own. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

- "Matthew's use of the old term 'Canaanite' shows that he cannot forget her ancestry: now a descendant of Israel's ancient enemies comes to the Jewish Messiah for blessing." (Carson, cited at EnduringWord.com)
- Ellicott suggests she may have heard of Jesus earlier: among the crowd at the Sermon on the Plain were people "from the sea-coast of Tyre and Sidon" (Luke 6:17). (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

## vv. 23-24 — Jesus' Silence and Apparent Rejection

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus at first answered "not a word." The disciples urged Him to "send her away" — likely meaning "give her what she wants so she'll leave" (the same verb is used in Luke 2:29 for a dismissal with desire satisfied). Jesus responded, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" — defining His earthly mission's primary scope. This echoes His instructions in Matthew 10:6. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org; Bible.org)

- Ellicott offers a notable alternative interpretation: rather than a "simulated harshness" to test faith, Ellicott suggests we see "the prevailing power of prayer working on the sympathy of Christ, and leading Him to pass beyond the ordinary limits of His appointed work." On this view, Jesus' silence reflected a real inner conflict between compassion and the normal limitation of His ministry. (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)
- "As Augustine says, 'The Word spoke not a word,' and that was so unlike him." (Spurgeon, cited at EnduringWord.com)

**Denominational Note — Reformed Baptist (DesiringGod/Piper):** "Jesus says, 'I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.' Now he said that when a Syrophoenician woman... came and asked him to heal her daughter... And she said, 'Yes, Lord, even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table.' And he said, 'For that, I'll heal your daughter.' In other words, 'That's great faith. I love that kind of humility. I don't care where it comes from.'" (DesiringGod.org)

## vv. 25-27 — Persistent Faith; Children's Bread and Dogs

**Traditional Reading:** The woman knelt and worshipped, praying the simplest of prayers: "Lord, help me!" Jesus answered with what sounds harsh: "It is not right to take the children's bread and toss it to the dogs." However, the Greek word for "dogs" here is *kynaria* — a diminutive form meaning "little dogs" or household pets, not the wild, unclean street dogs (Gk. *kynes*) that Jews typically associated with Gentiles. This softened the traditional slur. The woman seized on this opening: "Yes, Lord, yet even the little dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table." She accepted her place but pressed her claim. (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

- Ellicott notes a strikingly parallel story in the Talmud: a man named Jonathan appealed to Rabbi Jehudah during a famine, saying, "Feed me as a dog is fed, who eats of the crumbs of the feast," and the Rabbi granted his request. (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)
- "She would not give over, though he gave her three repulses. So as she said, like Jacob, 'I will not let thee go, until thou bless me.'" (Poole, cited at EnduringWord.com)
- "Dear friend, possibly someone has whispered in your ear, 'Suppose you are not one of the elect.' Well, that was very much what our Lord's expression meant to her... Notice that this woman does not battle with that truth at all... she just goes on praying, 'Lord, help me!'" (Spurgeon, cited at EnduringWord.com)
- Bible.org notes: "Her words open the old wounds... She is well aware of the ancient rivalry between the Jews and the Canaanites. She believes He is the promised Messiah; but if that is true, then He is to her a Jewish king, 'Son of David.'" (Bible.org)

## v. 28 — "Great Is Your Faith!"

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus exclaimed, "O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire." This is unique — Jesus never directly addressed anyone else with these words (He spoke of the centurion's great faith *about* him to the crowd, Matthew 8:10, but here He spoke directly *to* her). Both recipients of the "great faith" commendation were Gentiles. Her daughter was healed "from that very hour." (EnduringWord.com)

- "Great faith may be found in unexpected places... Great faith is sometimes measured from its disadvantages... Faith is often greatest when it is expressed on behalf of someone else's need." (EnduringWord.com)

**Denominational Note — Reformed (DesiringGod / Piper):** "We learn from the centurion and the Canaanite woman that poverty of spirit is right at the very heart of what true faith is." (DesiringGod.org)

**Denominational Note — Methodist/Wesleyan:** The Wesleyan tradition emphasises this passage as a model of persevering, humble intercessory prayer that will not take "no" for an answer — a pattern of "prevailing prayer." (Implied by the homiletic tradition; the Seedbed.com and Wesley.nnU.edu sites were not directly accessible in searches.)

## vv. 29-31 — Healings by the Sea of Galilee

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus returned to Galilee, went up a mountain, and sat — the posture of a teacher. Great crowds brought the lame, blind, crippled, mute, and "many others," laying them at His feet. He healed them all. The crowd was amazed and "glorified the God of Israel." This phrase may suggest the crowd included Gentiles from the Decapolis region (cf. Mark 7:31, where Jesus travelled through Sidon to the Decapolis). (EnduringWord.com; Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

- Ellicott: "Here we get a great aggregate of miracles, unrecorded in detail, working on the minds of the multitude, and leading them to repeated utterances of praise in the form of a doxology — they 'glorified the God of Israel.'" (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

## vv. 32-39 — The Feeding of the Four Thousand

**Traditional Reading:** This is a distinct miracle from the feeding of the 5,000 (Matthew 14). Differences: here there were 4,000 men (not 5,000), seven loaves (not five), seven baskets of leftovers (not twelve), and the crowd had been with Jesus three days (not one). The word for "basket" here is *spyris* (a large hamper, the kind used to lower Paul over the wall in Acts 9:25), whereas in the 5,000 it was *kophinos* (a small hand-basket). Jesus expressed compassion — the crowd had been with Him three days without food. The disciples' question ("Where in this desolate place...?") suggests they had not yet fully learned from the earlier miracle. Jesus gave thanks, broke the bread, and the disciples distributed. All ate and were satisfied. (EnduringWord.com)

- EnduringWord.com sees this as a feeding of predominantly Gentiles (in the Decapolis region), demonstrating that "Gentiles received far more than mere crumbs from His table and foreshadowing the Messianic banquet open to all."
- Some critical scholars treat this as a doublet of the feeding of the 5,000, but the two accounts have distinct details (Ellicott on StudyLight.org addresses this and rejects the critical view).

**Modern Scholarship Note:** Some modern critical scholars view the two feeding miracles as variant accounts of the same event. Ellicott acknowledges this view but does not endorse it; the distinct details (different numbers, different baskets, different locations) argue for two separate events (Ellicott on StudyLight.org).

**Denominational Note — Pentecostal/Charismatic (EnduringWord/Guzik):** The miracle demonstrates that Jesus' compassion extends to physical needs and that He can multiply limited resources when placed in His hands — a principle often applied to provision and giving in Pentecostal teaching.

## v. 39 — Departure to Magadan

**Traditional Reading:** After dismissing the crowds, Jesus crossed by boat to "the region of Magadan" (called Magdala in some manuscripts and Dalmanutha in Mark 8:10). This is near the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. Ellicott identifies it with "the modern Ain-el-Bârideh, the 'cold fountain,' a glen which opens upon the lake about a mile from Magdala." (Ellicott on StudyLight.org)

---

## Summary of Major Themes Across Traditions

| Theme | Shared Emphasis |
|-------|----------------|
| **Tradition vs. Scripture** | All Protestant traditions warn against elevating human traditions to equality with Scripture |
| **Heart-defilement** | Universal: sin proceeds from within; external religion cannot cleanse a corrupt heart |
| **Canaanite woman** | Celebrated as a model of persevering, humble faith across all traditions |
| **Corban practice** | Seen as a clear example of religious casuistry evading God's clear commands |
| **Two feedings** | Affirmed as distinct miracles by conservative traditions; viewed as doublets by some critical scholars |

---

**Sources used:** EnduringWord.com (Pentecostal/Charismatic); Ellicott's Commentary on StudyLight.org (older Anglican); Gill's Exposition on StudyLight.org (Reformed Baptist); PreceptAustin.org (Evangelical, drawing on MacArthur, Spurgeon, Barclay, Robertson, Utley and others); Matthew Henry on BibleHub.com (Reformed/Puritan); DesiringGod.org (Reformed Baptist/Piper); Bible.org (Evangelical). No Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Methodist-specific, or prosperity-gospel sources were retrieved from the allowed sites within the search and fetch limits for this chapter.
